newsitem.title: UK: Maestro Solti celebrates 50 years of recording.
newsitem.headline: Maestro Solti celebrates 50 years of recording.

text.p: Musical maestro Sir Georg Solti on Wednesday celebrated the 50th anniversary of his first symphonic recording as a conductor when "I was bad, the orchestra was bad, everything was bad".
But, as he approaches his 85th birthday, one of the world's most prolific and peripatetic conductors has no intention of slowing down.
Solti, who has conducted 45 operas among his 250 recordings, plans to make four more -- Pelleas and Melisande, Wozzeck, The Queen of Spades and Idomeneo.

The Hungarian-born conductor, being honoured by a special presentation at the Royal Academy of Arts of his first Decca recording contract, said in an interview: "I would like to do all four operas if I live long enough."
Solti, who has won more Grammy music awards than Michael Jackson or Madonna, told his record company: "I look forward to continuing our unique partnership into the 21st century."

Reflecting on his golden anniversary, he said: "It was not easy in the beginning to be in all sorts of people's shadow and I don't only mean (Herbert von) Karajan since (Leonard) Bernstein and many others were more important in those days."
His debut symphonic recording was Beethoven's Egmont Overture with the Zurich Tonhalle Orchestra. He refuses to view it through the rose-coloured spectacles of nostalgia.
"I was bad, the orchestra was bad, everything was bad. But obviously I showed that I could conduct," he said.
Classical music's most successful recording star, who won international fame for his work at London's Covent Garden Opera House and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, insists he has mellowed with age.
"It is really important you are not a megalomaniac when making recordings. You have to concentrate on the bad takes and why they are bad, which is a very complicated matter.
"In the heat of a recording session it can sometimes be difficult to judge between a good and a bad take," said Solti, a child prodigy at the piano whose family was wiped out in the Holocaust.
His most famous recording was the entire Ring cycle with the Vienna Philharmonic. It took seven years to complete.

Solti, who took up British nationality in 1972, is accepting bookings beyond the millenium and the conductor who has always refused to be a specialist said: "Our repertory is simply endless so one must see what one can do."
